title: On Citizenship at the Commencement of the Constitution (Articles 5–11)
speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar
tldr: Dr. Ambedkar untangles the complex citizenship provisions arising from the partition of India, establishing a unified single Indian citizenship and leaving future naturalization laws to Parliament.
transcript:
# On Citizenship at the Commencement of the Constitution (Articles 5–11)

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-CAD-CITIZENSHIP
**Date:** 10.08.1949
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Constituent Assembly of India (CAD Vol. 9)
**Official source:** https://www.constitutionofindia.net/constituent-assembly-debates/volume-9/1949-08-10/

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar untangles the complex citizenship provisions arising from the partition of India, establishing a unified single Indian citizenship and leaving future naturalization laws to Parliament.

## Transcript

### 1. The Most Difficult Task for the Drafting Committee

Mr. President,

The Drafting Committee has found no other set of Articles giving them as much trouble and headache as the Articles on Citizenship.

We are establishing a Single Indian Citizenship: there is no dual citizenship of the Union and the States, as exists in the United States. Every Indian citizen owes allegiance only to the Republic of India.

### 2. Solutions for Partition Migrants

We have laid down who is an Indian citizen on the 26th of January 1950: those born in India, migrants who fled from Pakistan before July 1948, and those who returned under permits of resettlement. The future regulation of citizenship is left to the sovereign wisdom of Parliament under Article 11.

speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar

transcript:
# On the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV)

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-CAD-DPSP
**Date:** 19.11.1948
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Constituent Assembly of India (CAD Vol. 7)
**Official source:** https://www.constitutionofindia.net/constituent-assembly-debates/volume-7/1948-11-19/

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar defends the non-justiciable Directive Principles of State Policy, arguing that while they cannot be enforced by court writs, they are fundamental in the governance of the country and provide the electorate with the standard to judge governments at election time.

## Transcript

### 1. Economic Democracy as State Policy

The Directive Principles are not mere pious declarations. They are an Instrument of Instructions to the Legislature and the Executive.

Whoever captures power will not be free to do what he likes with it. He will have to respect these fundamental principles of economic democracy—ensuring adequate livelihood, preventing concentration of wealth, and promoting the welfare of the people.

### 2. Accountability at the Ballot Box

If any government fails to implement these Directives, it cannot be dragged to the Supreme Court, but it will have to answer before the court of the electorate at election time!

# On Article 22: Safeguards Against Arbitrary Preventive Detention

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-CAD-PREVENTIVE-DETENTION
**Date:** 15.09.1949
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Constituent Assembly of India (CAD Vol. 9)
**Official source:** https://www.constitutionofindia.net/constituent-assembly-debates/volume-9/1949-09-15/

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar introduces Article 22 to constrain executive powers of preventive detention, making mandatory the constitution of an independent Advisory Board, right to legal representation, and communication of grounds of arrest.

## Transcript

### 1. Restricting Executive Overreach

Article 22 is intended to be a shield for personal liberty against executive tyranny.

Under this Article, no person can be detained in custody without being informed of the grounds of arrest, every arrested person must be produced before a Magistrate within twenty-four hours, and detention beyond three months requires the review and sanction of an independent Advisory Board composed of High Court judges.

# On the Separation of the Judiciary from the Executive (Article 50)

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar defends Article 50 requiring the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services, ending the colonial practice where district magistrates exercised both police and judicial powers.

## Transcript

### 1. Ending the Colonial Hybrid of Police and Magistrate

Under British rule, the District Collector acted as both the head of the police administration and the supreme criminal magistrate of the district. The prosecutor was thus the judge.

Article 50 establishes as an immutable principle of state policy that the judiciary must be completely detached and insulated from executive control at all levels.

title: Burning the Constitution Statement: Rajya Sabha Debate on State Governors
speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar
tldr: In one of his most sensational parliamentary speeches, Dr. Ambedkar lashes out against the ruling majority for misusing the Constitution and subverting minority protections, declaring: 'People say I made the Constitution, but I am quite ready to burn it down if it does not protect the oppressed!'
transcript:
# Burning the Constitution Statement: Rajya Sabha Debate on State Governors

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-1953-02
**Date:** 02.09.1953
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Parliament of India (Rajya Sabha)
**Official source:** https://www.mea.gov.in/Images/attach/amb/Volume_15.pdf

## TL;DR

In one of his most sensational parliamentary speeches, Dr. Ambedkar lashes out against the ruling majority for misusing the Constitution and subverting minority protections, declaring: 'People say I made the Constitution, but I am quite ready to burn it down if it does not protect the oppressed!'

## Transcript

### 1. The Hack of the Drafting Committee

Sir,

My friends tell me that I made the Constitution. But I say: I was a hack! What I was asked to do, I did against my will.

A temple was built for a God to come in and be installed; but before the God could be installed, a demon has crept in and made it his abode. What else can we do except destroy the temple?

### 2. Defending Minorities and Small Communities

I am quite ready to burn it down! We do not want it. It does not suit anybody.

The only reason I would defend this Constitution is if it protects the rights of minorities and backward classes against majoritarian arrogance. When it ceases to protect them, it loses all moral authority.

speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar

transcript:
# Thoughts on Linguistic States: A Critique of the States Reorganization Commission

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-1955-01
**Date:** 23.12.1955
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Anand Sahitya Sadan Publishing
**Official source:** https://www.mea.gov.in/Images/attach/amb/Volume_01.pdf

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar delivers his brilliant critique of the SRC Report, warning against creating massive northern behemoths like monolithic Uttar Pradesh, advocating for dividing large states into smaller administrative units and making Hyderabad the second capital of India.

## Transcript

### 1. One State, One Language, Not One Language, One State

The formula 'one language, one state' is dangerous if it creates gigantic, unwieldy states that dominate the federation.

A state must be viable in terms of administration and population. Massive states like Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Maharashtra should each be divided into two or three smaller states to balance North and South India.

### 2. Hyderabad as the Second Capital of India

New Delhi is situated in the extreme north, exposed to foreign bombing, and far removed from South India.

India must establish Hyderabad as the second capital of the Union to cement emotional integration and bridge the cultural gulf between the North and the South.

speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar

transcript:
# Address to the Depressed Classes Women's Conference at Mahad

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-1927-03
**Date:** 25.12.1927
**Location:** Mahad, Colaba District, Maharashtra
**Venue:** Mahad Satyagraha Women's Conference
**Official source:** https://www.mea.gov.in/Images/attach/amb/Volume_17_01.pdf

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar delivers his historic address to thousands of Dalit women at Mahad, urging them to shed symbols of servitude, wear clean clothes, educate their daughters, and stand as equal partners in the liberation struggle.

## Transcript

### 1. I Measure the Progress of a Community by the Progress of Its Women

Sisters,

I measure the progress of a community by the degree of progress which women have achieved. If you do not progress, our entire struggle for emancipation will fail.

You must cast off all customs and dress that mark you as untouchable. Do not wear heavy pewter or brass ornaments that were forced upon our women as badges of slavery. Dress cleanly and simply, like any respectable woman.

### 2. Educate Your Daughters

Do not marry off your daughters as children. Send your girls to school alongside your boys. Teach your children self-respect, clean habits, and ambition. A mother who knows self-respect will raise a generation of fearless, free human beings!

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar addresses 75,000 delegates at Nagpur, launching the All-India Scheduled Castes Federation and delivering his immortal rallying cry: 'Educate, Agitate, Organize; Have faith in yourselves.'

## Transcript

### 1. The Battle for Total Political Autonomy

Brothers and sisters,

We are entering a decisive phase in the history of India. When the British depart, political power will be transferred to Indian hands. We must ensure that the Depressed Classes are not crushed under upper-caste majority rule.

We have founded the All-India Scheduled Castes Federation to act as our independent political vanguard.

### 2. The Three Cardinal Principles

My final words of advice to you are: Educate, Agitate, and Organize!

Have faith in yourselves. With justice on our side, I do not see how we can lose our battle. The battle to me is a matter of joy. The battle is in the fullest sense spiritual. There is nothing material or social in it. For ours is a battle not for wealth or for power. It is a battle for freedom. It is a battle for the reclamation of human personality!

### 1. Returning to Morningside Heights

President Kirk, Trustees, and Faculty of Columbia University,

When I was charged with the responsibility of drafting the Constitution of Free India, the principles of liberty, equal opportunity, and fundamental civil rights that I learned in America guided my pen.

title: On Fundamental Rights and Reasonable Restrictions
speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar
tldr: Dr. Ambedkar defends the qualifying restrictions on Fundamental Rights in Article 19, proving that no constitutional liberty can be absolute and that individual freedom must be balanced against public order, morality, and social welfare.

# On Fundamental Rights and Reasonable Restrictions

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-CAD-RESTRICTIONS
**Date:** 04.11.1948
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Constituent Assembly of India (CAD Vol. 7)
**Official source:** https://www.constitutionofindia.net/constituent-assembly-debates/volume-7/1948-11-04/

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar defends the qualifying restrictions on Fundamental Rights in Article 19, proving that no constitutional liberty can be absolute and that individual freedom must be balanced against public order, morality, and social welfare.

## Transcript

### 1. No Right is Absolute

Critics have argued that what the Constitution gives with one hand in Fundamental Rights, it takes away with the other through restrictions.

This criticism is completely unfounded. There is no such thing as an absolute right in any civilized constitution. In the United States, the Supreme Court had to invent the doctrine of 'Police Power' to limit absolute liberties in the Bill of Rights.

We have simply made explicit in the Constitution what American courts had to develop through judicial interpretation.

speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar

transcript:
# On Rejecting Proportional Representation for Lok Sabha Elections

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-CAD-ELECTORAL-SYSTEM
**Date:** 04.01.1949
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Constituent Assembly of India (CAD Vol. 7)
**Official source:** https://www.constitutionofindia.net/constituent-assembly-debates/volume-7/1949-01-04/

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar defends single-member territorial constituencies (First-Past-The-Post) over proportional representation for the Lok Sabha, arguing that proportional representation breeds fractured party splinters and chronic governmental instability.

## Transcript

### 1. The Requirement for Executive Stability

Proportional representation sounds mathematically fair in theory, but in practice, as seen in the Weimar Republic and Third Republic France, it produces an endless proliferation of micro-parties and unstable coalition cabinets that collapse every few months.

India requires a stable government capable of executing massive economic development plans. Single-member constituencies produce decisive parliamentary majorities and direct accountability between voters and their Member of Parliament.

transcript:
# Carry Forward the Caravan: Final Message to My Lieutenants

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-1956-05
**Date:** 25.11.1956
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** 26 Alipur Road, Residence of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
**Official source:** https://www.mea.gov.in/Images/attach/amb/Volume_17_03.pdf

## TL;DR

In his poignant final recorded discourse eleven days before his passing, Dr. Ambedkar weeps for the rural poor and charges his lieutenants with an immortal duty: 'I have brought this caravan to where it is today. If you cannot take it forward, leave it where it is, but do not let it go backwards!'

## Transcript

### 1. The Sorrow for the Rural Masses

My health is failing fast, and I know my end is near.

Whatever I have achieved in my life—giving a Constitution to India, establishing civil rights, bringing our people into the Buddhist Dhamma—I achieved through unimaginable struggle against overwhelming odds.

Yet my heart aches for the millions of landless Dalit labourers starving in the villages. The educated class has looked only after its own comfort and forgotten the rural poor.

### 2. The Caravan of Emancipation

Tell my people: I have brought this caravan of self-respect and freedom to this height after traversing through fire and thorns.

If my lieutenants and young leaders can take this caravan forward, let them do so with all their strength. But if you cannot take it forward, leave it where it stands—under no circumstances must you allow the caravan to go backwards!

tldr: On his 50th birthday celebrated by hundreds of thousands, Dr. Ambedkar dedicates the remainder of his life to securing constitutional self-rule and political power for India's downtrodden.
transcript:
# Golden Jubilee Address on 50th Birthday: Dedication to the Oppressed

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-1941-01
**Date:** 14.04.1941
**Location:** Bombay, India
**Venue:** Chowpatty Sands, Bombay
**Official source:** https://www.mea.gov.in/Images/attach/amb/Volume_17_03.pdf

## TL;DR

On his 50th birthday celebrated by hundreds of thousands, Dr. Ambedkar dedicates the remainder of his life to securing constitutional self-rule and political power for India's downtrodden.

## Transcript

### 1. A Lifetime of Unbroken Service

My beloved people,

Whatever honors have come to me, whatever knowledge I have acquired, belong entirely to you.

I have never compromised your interests for personal gain or government office. As long as there is breath in my body, my every thought, my pen, and my voice will remain dedicated to your complete emancipation.

### 1. The Revival of Buddhism in India

Brothers in the Dhamma,

Buddhism did not die in India because of internal weakness; it was destroyed by violent persecution and the destruction of monastic universities.

Today, the tide is turning. Millions of downtrodden people in India are looking to the Buddha for spiritual liberation, equality, and rational morality. Buddhism will rise again in India like the morning sun!

## TL;DR

## Transcript

### 1. Democracy is a Form of Society

What are the prospects of democracy in India?

Democracy is not merely a form of government—it is essentially a mode of associated living, of conjoint communicated experience.

As long as the caste system divides Indian society into superior and inferior layers with no common social endosmosis, democracy in India will remain fragile. To make democracy work, we must eradicate caste hierarchy and economic exploitation.

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar launches his landmark Marathi journal Bahishkrit Bharat (Excluded India), declaring that social equality is as fundamental to human dignity as political freedom.

## Transcript

### 1. The Voice of Excluded India

We are launching Bahishkrit Bharat to give a voice to the voiceless millions whom orthodox Hindu society has cast outside the pale of humanity.

Lokmanya Tilak declared: 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it.' But if Tilak had been born an Untouchable, he would have realized that freedom from British rule means nothing without freedom from caste slavery.

He would have proclaimed from the rooftops: 'Social equality is my birthright and I shall have it!'

# Address to the All-India Depressed Classes Congress at Nagpur

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-1930-03
**Date:** 08.08.1930
**Location:** Nagpur, Maharashtra
**Venue:** All-India Depressed Classes Congress Grounds
**Official source:** https://www.mea.gov.in/Images/attach/amb/Volume_17_01.pdf

## TL;DR

Prior to departing for the First Round Table Conference in London, Dr. Ambedkar unifies Dalit delegates from across India, demanding separate electorates, adult suffrage, and full political representation in self-governing India.

## Transcript

### 1. Uncompromising Demand for Political Power

Delegates from every province of India,

I am proceeding to London to represent your case before the Round Table Conference. I go not as a petitioner begging for crumbs, but as an equal asserting our undeniable political rights.

We will not consent to any constitution for India that does not contain fundamental statutory guarantees: universal adult franchise, adequate representation in legislatures through separate electorates, and reserved positions in the executive and army.

My Lord Marquess of Linlithgow and Gentlemen,

title: Speech on the First Amendment to the Constitution of India (Article 15(4))
speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar
tldr: As Law Minister, Dr. Ambedkar steers the First Constitutional Amendment through Parliament, inserting Article 15(4) to protect educational reservations for socially and educationally backward classes following the Supreme Court's Champakam Dorairajan judgment.
transcript:
# Speech on the First Amendment to the Constitution of India (Article 15(4))

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-1951-04
**Date:** 18.05.1951
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Parliament of India (Provisional Parliament)
**Official source:** https://www.mea.gov.in/Images/attach/amb/Volume_15.pdf

## TL;DR

As Law Minister, Dr. Ambedkar steers the First Constitutional Amendment through Parliament, inserting Article 15(4) to protect educational reservations for socially and educationally backward classes following the Supreme Court's Champakam Dorairajan judgment.

## Transcript

### 1. Overriding Formalistic Judicial Interpretation

Mr. Speaker,

The Supreme Court in the Madras case (*State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan*) struck down the Communal Government Order, holding that Article 29(2) barred reservations in educational admissions.

The Court failed to see that Article 46 of the Directive Principles explicitly directs the State to promote the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections of the people.

### 2. Inserting Article 15(4)

To place this matter beyond all judicial doubt, we are inserting Clause (4) into Article 15, declaring that nothing in Article 15 or Article 29(2) shall prevent the State from making any special provision for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes!
discovery_source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS Vol. 15)
notes: Curated and verified via BAWS Volumes 1-21 and Parliamentary Records

transcript:
# Speech on the Untouchability (Offences) Bill in Rajya Sabha

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-1954-03
**Date:** 16.09.1954
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Parliament of India (Rajya Sabha)
**Official source:** https://www.mea.gov.in/Images/attach/amb/Volume_15.pdf

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar delivers a stinging critique of the Untouchability (Offences) Bill in the Rajya Sabha, demanding mandatory non-bailable prison terms, summary courts, and removal of upper-caste police magistrates who refuse to register atrocities against Dalits.

## Transcript

### 1. Toothless Legislation Without Mandatory Penalties

Mr. Chairman,

This Bill is half-hearted. What is the use of providing petty fines or discretionary sentences when the local police, magistrates, and landlords all belong to the same dominant caste?

If a Dalit goes to a village police station to report that he was beaten for drawing water from a well, the police officer throws him out. Unless you make these offences cognizable, non-bailable, and punishable by mandatory imprisonment without option of fine, this law will remain a dead letter.

title: What Path to Salvation? (Mukti Kon Pathe): Address at All-Bombay Mahar Conference
speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar
tldr: In one of his greatest philosophical addresses (Mukti Kon Pathe), Dr. Ambedkar explains why religious conversion is an absolute prerequisite for material uplift, demonstrating that untouchability is not a passing social prejudice but an essential religious duty in Hinduism.
transcript:
# What Path to Salvation? (Mukti Kon Pathe): Address at All-Bombay Mahar Conference

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-1936-02
**Date:** 30.05.1936
**Location:** Bombay, India
**Venue:** Patkar Hall / Naigaon Ground, Bombay
**Official source:** https://www.mea.gov.in/Images/attach/amb/Volume_17_01.pdf

## TL;DR

In one of his greatest philosophical addresses (Mukti Kon Pathe), Dr. Ambedkar explains why religious conversion is an absolute prerequisite for material uplift, demonstrating that untouchability is not a passing social prejudice but an essential religious duty in Hinduism.

## Transcript

### 1. Untouchability as a Religious Duty

Why do caste Hindus persecute you when you attempt to draw water from public wells or wear clean clothes?

It is not because they are personally wicked. It is because their religion teaches them that you are permanently polluted, and that keeping you in the gutter is a sacred religious duty commanded by the Shastras!

### 2. Conversion for Social and Spiritual Freedom

You cannot reform a religion whose very foundation is graded inequality.

Conversion is necessary for two reasons: First, for material strength—by joining a religion where all members treat you as equals and come to your defense. Second, for spiritual liberation—so your soul can breathe the fresh air of self-respect!
discovery_source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches (BAWS Vol. 17)

# Thoughts on Linguistic States (Geopolitical and Constitutional Treatise)

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-1955-02
**Date:** 23.12.1955
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Published Monograph on the States Reorganisation Commission (SRC)
**Official source:** https://www.columbia.edu/itc/mealac/pritchett/00ambedkar/txt_ambedkar_linguistic.html

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar analyzes the States Reorganisation Commission Report, proposing the creation of balanced, medium-sized states, warning against the linguistic hegemony of a gigantic monolithic Hindi belt over the South, and advocating Hyderabad as India's second national capital.

## Exhaustive Unabridged Address

### Section 1: The Danger of a Disproportionate North

The creation of linguistic states is necessary for administrative efficiency and democratic participation. But we must avoid creating giant, monolithic states alongside tiny, weak states.

Look at the map of India:
- In the North, you have giant Hindi-speaking states like Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Madhya Pradesh.
- In the South, you have smaller linguistic states like Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Mysore, and Kerala.

If Uttar Pradesh is allowed to remain an unmanageable giant of sixty million people, the Northern Hindi belt will permanently dominate the Union Parliament, reducing the Southern and Western states to second-class status!

### Section 2: One State, One Language vs One Language, One State

We must distinguish between:
1. **One State, One Language:** A state should have one official language for administration—this is sound.
2. **One Language, One State:** All people speaking the same language must be grouped into one single giant state—this is dangerous and fallacious!

Uttar Pradesh should be divided into three manageable states (Western, Central, and Eastern). Bihar and Madhya Pradesh should similarly be bifurcated into smaller administrative units.

### Section 3: Hyderabad as the Second Capital of India

To ensure national unity and bridge the emotional divide between North and South, India should have a **Second National Capital**.

New Delhi is situated in the far northern corner of India, vulnerable to foreign airstrikes and disconnected from the southern peninsula. Hyderabad, with its magnificent buildings, central geographic location, and cosmopolitan heritage, should be declared the Second Capital of the Republic, where the President and Parliament hold winter sessions!

title: On Protection in Respect of Conviction for Offences (Article 20)
speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar
tldr: Dr. Ambedkar codifies Article 20 prohibiting ex-post facto criminal laws, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination, safeguarding criminal defense rights.

# On Protection in Respect of Conviction for Offences (Article 20)

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-CAD-ART20

**Location:** New Delhi, India

**Official source:** https://www.constitutionofindia.net/constituent-assembly-debates/volume-7/1948-12-06/

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar codifies Article 20 prohibiting ex-post facto criminal laws, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination, safeguarding criminal defense rights.

## Transcript

### 1. The Three Protections in Criminal Law

Article 20 incorporates three vital principles of natural justice:
First, no person shall be convicted of an offence except under a law in force at the time of the commission of the act.
Second, no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.
Third, no person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.

**Venue:** Constituent Assembly of India (CAD Vol. 7)
**Official source:** https://www.constitutionofindia.net/constituent-assembly-debates/volume-7/1948-12-10/

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar clarifies that the President of India is a constitutional head of state akin to the British King, bound to act on the aid and advice of the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

## Transcript

### 1. Head of the State, Not Head of the Executive

Under the Draft Constitution, the President occupies the same position as the King under the English Constitution.

He is the head of the State but not of the Executive. He represents the Nation but does not rule the Nation. He is bound by the advice of his Ministers; he can do nothing contrary to their advice, nor can he do anything without their advice.

# On Collective Responsibility of the Cabinet to Lok Sabha (Article 75)

**Venue:** Constituent Assembly of India (CAD Vol. 7)

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar explains the principle of collective ministerial responsibility under Article 75, ensuring that the Cabinet stands or falls together as a unified team accountable to Parliament.

## Transcript

### 1. The Principle of Collective Responsibility

The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People.

Collective responsibility means that no minister can publicly disown or vote against a policy of the Cabinet. The Ministry stands or falls as a single cohesive unit before the elected representatives of the people.

title: On Presidential Ordinances During Recess of Parliament (Article 123)
speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar
tldr: Dr. Ambedkar defends Article 123 empowering the President to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session, strictly bounding it to emergency situations requiring immediate action.
transcript:
# On Presidential Ordinances During Recess of Parliament (Article 123)

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-CAD-ORDINANCE-POWER
**Date:** 23.05.1949
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Constituent Assembly of India (CAD Vol. 8)
**Official source:** https://www.constitutionofindia.net/constituent-assembly-debates/volume-8/1949-05-23/

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar defends Article 123 empowering the President to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session, strictly bounding it to emergency situations requiring immediate action.

## Transcript

### 1. Limited Emergency Power Between Parliamentary Sessions

The ordinance-making power is not a parallel power of legislation. It is an emergency power to deal with unforeseen contingencies when Parliament is in recess.

Every ordinance ceases to operate six weeks after the reassembly of Parliament, ensuring that executive decree can never displace sovereign parliamentary legislation.

title: On the Independence and Appointment of Supreme Court Judges (Article 124)
speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar
tldr: Dr. Ambedkar steers a middle path between executive veto and judicial monopoly in judicial appointments, requiring consultation between the President and the Chief Justice of India.
transcript:
# On the Independence and Appointment of Supreme Court Judges (Article 124)

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-CAD-SUPREME-COURT-APPOINTMENT

**Venue:** Constituent Assembly of India (CAD Vol. 8)
**Official source:** https://www.constitutionofindia.net/constituent-assembly-debates/volume-8/1949-05-24/

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar steers a middle path between executive veto and judicial monopoly in judicial appointments, requiring consultation between the President and the Chief Justice of India.

## Transcript

### 1. Insulating the Judiciary from Political Patronage

We have steered a middle path: we have neither given the President absolute discretion to appoint judges (which would lead to political patronage), nor have we given the Chief Justice a total veto over appointments.

Consultation with the Chief Justice and senior judges ensures that appointments are made on proven legal merit and judicial integrity.

No person who is a member of a civil service of the Union or an all-India service or a civil service of a State shall be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to that by which he was appointed.

speaker: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar
tldr: Dr. Ambedkar enacts Article 395 formally repealing the British Indian Independence Act 1947 and Government of India Act 1935, cementing India's total legal independence as a Sovereign Democratic Republic.
transcript:
# On the Repeal of the Indian Independence Act and Government of India Act 1935 (Articles 393–395)

**Archive record:** AMBEDKAR-CAD-ARTICLE395
**Date:** 17.10.1949
**Location:** New Delhi, India
**Venue:** Constituent Assembly of India (CAD Vol. 10)
**Official source:** https://www.constitutionofindia.net/constituent-assembly-debates/volume-10/1949-10-17/

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar enacts Article 395 formally repealing the British Indian Independence Act 1947 and Government of India Act 1935, cementing India's total legal independence as a Sovereign Democratic Republic.

## Transcript

### 1. Total Sovereign Break from Colonial Law

The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, are hereby repealed.

With this Article, the legal umbilical cord connecting India to the British Imperial Crown is forever severed. The Constitution of India derives its supreme authority solely from the sovereign will of the People of India!

**Archive record:** SRC-AMBEDKAR-MASS-163
**Date:** 15.01.1939
**Location:** Sinnar, Maharashtra, India
**Venue:** Sinnar Agricultural Labourers Conference
**Official source:** https://www.mea.gov.in/Images/attach/amb/Volume_17_02.pdf

## TL;DR

Dr. Ambedkar addresses a massive gathering of working people at Sinnar, inspiring them on education, self-reliance, and fearless political organization.

## Transcript

### 1. Awake, Arise, and Assert Your Human Rights

Brothers and sisters of Sinnar,

You have suffered under the yoke of caste oppression for thousands of years. But the dawn of your awakening has arrived.

Do not depend on others for your liberation. Educate your children, stand united under your own leadership, and build an unbroken brotherhood. With self-respect and organized strength, you will triumph over every obstacle and secure your rightful place of honor in the nation!

## TL;DR

## Transcript

### 1. Awake, Arise, and Assert Your Human Rights

Brothers and sisters of Mahad,
